transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Thanks for seeing me. 

Well, what brings me in is that I keep getting these thoughts. I manage IT systems, and I just have this constant fear that if I miss one setting... or one access rule, or some warning sign, someone could get hurt or lose everything. And, I mean, part of me knows it’s irrational. But it hits me like I’m personally responsible, and I just can’t seem to move on from it.

When you have these fears about missing a setting or access rule, do you find yourself checking your work repeatedly, or do you feel driven to perform certain actions or routines to make sure nothing goes wrong?

Yeah, I do. I check things constantly. I’ll reread deployment plans, the audit logs... even old messages, just over and over. And it's not just the computer stuff, I do it with the door locks at work, too. 

A lot of the time, I find myself counting through the steps in my head while I check things, and I have to keep going until it finally feels... safe, I guess. It takes so long that I’ve actually stayed at the office for hours after everyone else leaves. I just can't walk away, because if I try to force myself to stop before the routine feels complete, I just start to panic.

latest_inference.note: Patient demonstrates clear obsessions (intrusive thoughts about system failures causing harm) with compulsions (repetitive checking, counting, need for routines to feel 'safe', inability to stop without panic). This is diagnostic for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. F41.1 (GAD), F41.9 (unspecified anxiety), and F48.1 (neurasthenia) are ruled out as they do not explain the specific obsessive-compulsive pattern with ritualistic behaviors.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with obsessive-compulsive disorder characterized by intrusive obsessions (fear of harm/loss due to missed IT settings) and compulsive rituals (repetitive checking of work, audit logs, door locks, and counting routines). Compulsions are performed to reduce anxiety and feel 'safe.' Symptoms cause significant functional impairment (extended work hours, inability to leave office), and the patient demonstrates insight that thoughts are irrational. F42.1 (OCD with predominantly compulsive acts) is most appropriate given the prominence of checking and counting compulsions.
